But broadly speaking, if you have a broad enough diversified basket, you'll make out like a bandit. And that was the cornerstone realization of what became a pretty incredible junk bond empire.
turns.zh: 那几乎成了一种时代精神（zeitgeist）。这不公平，其中有些公司确实很糟、有些会违约。但大体而言，只要你持有一个足够分散的组合，你就能赚得盆满钵满。而这，正是后来那个相当了不起的高收益债券（junk bond）帝国赖以建立的基石认知。

turns.en: Welcome to Top Traders Unplugged. In markets, success doesn't come from predicting what happens next. It comes from being prepared for what you can't predict. In each episode, we go deep with some of the world's most thoughtful minds in investing, economics and beyond to understand how they think, how they prepare and how they decide, and the experiences that shaped how they see the world. No noise, no shortcuts, just real conversations to help you think better and invest with confidence.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 Top Traders Unplugged。在市场里，成功并不来自预测接下来会发生什么，而来自为你无法预测的事做好准备。在每一期节目中，我们都会与投资、经济及其他领域里世界上最善于思考的一些头脑深入交流，去理解他们如何思考、如何准备、如何决策，以及那些塑造了他们看待世界方式的经历。没有噪音，没有捷径，只有真实的对话，帮助你更好地思考、更有信心地投资。

turns.en: Welcome everyone to Top Traders Unplugged. My name is Kevin Coldiron and I'm host of the Ideas Lab series where we talk authors of new books that help us understand and navigate the global economy. Our guest today is Robin Wigglesworth. He's a longtime financial journalist and currently editor of the Financial Times influential Alphaville blog. He's the author of the book Trillions, which traces the evolution and future of passive investing.
turns.zh: 欢迎大家来到 Top Traders Unplugged。我叫 Kevin Coldiron，是 Ideas Lab 系列的主持人，在这个系列里我们会对话那些写出了帮助我们理解和驾驭全球经济的新书的作者。今天的嘉宾是 Robin Wigglesworth。他是一位资深财经记者，目前担任《金融时报》（Financial Times）颇具影响力的 Alphaville 博客的主编。他也是《Trillions》一书的作者，那本书追溯了被动投资（passive investing）的演变与未来。

turns.en: And he's here today to talk about his brand new book coming out in September, of Fabulous Debt, the epic story of how bonds built the modern world. Robin, thanks so much for joining us and welcome to the show.
turns.zh: 他今天来是要聊聊他九月即将出版的全新著作《Fabulous Debt》——一部讲述债券如何缔造现代世界的史诗。Robin，非常感谢你加入我们，欢迎上节目。

turns.en: No, thanks for inviting me, Kevin. I've been looking forward to it.
turns.zh: 哪里，谢谢你邀请我，Kevin。我一直很期待这次上节目。

turns.en: First of all, I feel like I have to start off by congratulating you on your market timing. You've managed to release a book about the bond market just when pretty much all anyone can talk about is the bond market. How did you manage to pull that off?
turns.zh: 首先，我觉得我得先恭喜你的市场时机把握得太好了。你偏偏在几乎所有人都在谈论债券市场的时候，出了一本关于债券市场的书。你是怎么办到的？

turns.en: Well, Kevin, how dare you? The bond market is always interesting.
turns.zh: 哎，Kevin，你这话说的。债券市场一直都很有意思。

turns.en: Always. No, I mean, I was always worried because I finished the book just before Liberation Day in 2025. The first draft, I was like, oh my God, should we try to rush this out? And the publisher pointed out the multitude of logistical issues around this, but also just the fact that ideally a book, if there is something going on that is particularly pertinent, that's great.
turns.zh: 一直都是。不，我是说，我之前一直很担心，因为我在 2025 年'解放日'（Liberation Day）之前就完成了这本书的初稿。当时我心想，天哪，我们要不要赶紧把它推出去？出版方指出了围绕这个的种种后勤问题，但也说，理想情况下，如果正好有特别切题的事情发生，那当然是好事。

turns.en: But you write a book to stand the of time, so you can't try. And it's like market timing, you shouldn't try to go crazy doing so. But I felt always confident that there's always something interesting going on in the fixed income market somewhere in the world and low there is right now. Again, yeah.
turns.zh: 但你写一本书是为了让它经得起时间考验，所以你不能刻意去赶。这就跟择时（market timing）一样，你不该疯狂地去押注时点。但我一直很有信心：世界上固定收益市场（fixed income）的某个角落总有有意思的事情在发生，而现在果然就有。是的。

turns.en: Well, you know, it's interesting that you say that about your publisher because really, this is a history book. It's about the history of the bond market. And I'd actually like to start off with a, a quote about history. From your introduction,
turns.zh: 嗯，你提到你的出版方，这点很有意思，因为说到底，这是一本历史书，讲的是债券市场的历史。我其实想先从你引言里的一句关于历史的名言聊起。

turns.en: you quote Lytton Strachey, who was a biographer and I think also a close friend of Keynes, who says ignorance is the first prerequisite of the historian. And I'm curious how you interpret this because I have to say I've thought quite a lot about it since reading it. I mean, to me it means we should kind of clear our minds of preconceived notions when we think about history. But then on the other hand, if we're always clearing our minds, what is the value of learning history, right? I mean, what do we take away?
turns.zh: 你引用了 Lytton Strachey 的话，他是一位传记作家，我记得也是 Keynes 的密友，他说'无知是历史学家的第一先决条件'。我很好奇你怎么理解这句话，因为老实说，读了之后我琢磨了很久。对我来说，它的意思是我们思考历史时应该清空脑中那些先入为主的观念。可话说回来，如果我们总是在清空脑子，那学历史的价值又在哪里呢？我们到底能从中带走什么？

turns.en: So I'm curious just why you chose to use that quote and what it means to you.
turns.zh: 所以我很好奇，你为什么选了这句话，它对你意味着什么。

turns.en: It's a great question actually, because I thought a lot about it as well when I came across it in a different book. I mean, for me it has two meanings, both of which felt very relevant for this. One thing is, yes, start without those preconceived notions. I mean, we can't entirely ignore lessons, the history of the, sometimes the knee jerk prejudices we might have. But try to start, you know, from a place of ignorance because almost the journey also becomes more joyful than it's, you know, you're
turns.zh: 这其实是个很好的问题，因为我在另一本书里读到它时，也琢磨了很久。对我来说它有两层意思，两层都跟这本书很相关。一层是，对，从没有那些先入之见开始。我是说，我们无法完全无视历史的教训，也无视我们有时会有的那种条件反射式的偏见。但要试着从一种'无知'的状态出发，因为这样一来，这段旅程几乎也会变得更愉悦，你是在——

turns.en: discovering things for the first time or, or relearning things, or seeing things you thought you knew from a radically different perspective. The other part is also, you know, something that's relevant for certainly historians, but also just journalists in that the world is immensely complex and you know, we need to find a balance between sort of embracing that nuance, the complexity in writing about it, but also writing in a clear way that, you know, we need to kind of bring forth the core truth, as it were.
turns.zh: 第一次去发现一些东西，或者重新学习一些东西，或者从一个截然不同的视角去看你以为自己早已了解的事情。另一层意思，对历史学家当然相关，对记者也一样：世界极其复杂，我们需要在拥抱那种细微差别、那种复杂性去书写它，和用清晰的方式去写之间找到平衡，也就是说，我们需要把核心的真相呈现出来。

turns.en: I mean, not sort of stretch things, but, you know, maybe cut off stuff that's extraneous. I mean, you work in a financial environment a lot of like, for good traders, it's about cutting out stuff that isn't actually essential to hone in what actually matters.
turns.zh: 我不是说去夸大扭曲事实，而是也许要砍掉那些无关紧要的东西。你在金融环境里工作就知道，对优秀的交易员来说，关键在于剔除那些其实并不本质的东西，好聚焦于真正重要的部分。

turns.en: That doesn't mean you're not seeing an entire picture, but your focus, focusing on the factors that matter the most. For a journalist, like writing a thousand years of bond market history. There are so many, I guess, tech people who call it side quests I could have gone down and some of which broke my heart not to pursue. So I love writing about sovereign debt restructuring, countries going bankrupt, and there is a bit of that in the book, but I was going to have a whole section on it. And I realized it was fascinating,
turns.zh: 这不代表你没看到全局，而是你把注意力集中在最重要的因素上。对一个记者来说，比如要写一千年的债券市场历史，有太多——我想搞技术的人会叫它'支线任务'（side quests）——我本可以深入去写，其中有些我不得不放弃，真是让我心痛。我很喜欢写主权债务重组（sovereign debt restructuring）、国家破产这类话题，书里确实有一点，但我原本打算专门写一整节。后来我意识到它很迷人，

turns.en: especially to me, but it wasn't really that essential. Then there's the issue of linkers. The linking, like an inflation truth bond, were invented in the US Even before the US existed as a country. Massachusetts issued them. And they're fascinating as well. There's so many other aspects that are interesting that I didn't really.
turns.zh: 至少对我而言很迷人，但它并不是那么本质。还有通胀挂钩债券（linkers）的问题。这种通胀保值债券（inflation-linked bond）甚至在美国作为一个国家存在之前，就在美国被发明出来了。Massachusetts 发行过它们，同样很迷人。还有很多别的有意思的方面，我并没有真的——

turns.en: I felt I needed to clarify by simplifying and other things I didn't think I was going to write that I did end up writing about instead.
turns.zh: 我觉得有必要通过简化来讲清楚；还有一些我原以为不会去写的内容，最后反倒写了进去。

turns.en: Yeah, I appreciate that because I did get that sense in reading the book. There was a couple times where you're like, would really like to talk more about this, but we're going to go back to bonds.
turns.zh: 是啊，我很认同，因为读书时我确实有那种感觉。有那么几处你会觉得'真很想再多聊聊这个'，但接着又回到了债券本身。

turns.en: Well, this is it. I mean, when you write about something like this, it's so easy to get distracted. Like history of central banking, the history of money, history of financial markets more broadly. And sometimes I felt it unavoidable. So there's lots on Bretton woods and the Nixon shock. Just because I feel you can't really understand the trajectory of bonds in the 20th century when really we saw that was kind of the real. The ascent of the fixed income markets without really understanding the backdrop,
turns.zh: 嗯，就是这样。当你写这类题材时，太容易被带跑偏了，比如央行的历史、货币的历史、更广义的金融市场史。有时候我觉得这是难以避免的。所以书里有很多关于布雷顿森林体系（Bretton Woods）和尼克松冲击（Nixon shock）的内容。只是因为我觉得，如果不真正理解那个大背景，你就无法真正理解 20 世纪债券的轨迹——而 20 世纪其实正是固定收益市场真正的崛起期。

turns.en: but still kind of keeping the idea that the hero of my story is the bond, the humble bond. He usually is the protagonist and everything else is a supporting character.
turns.zh: 但我仍然坚持一个理念：我这个故事的主角是债券，是那只不起眼的债券。它通常是主人公，其他一切都是配角。

turns.en: Okay, well, let's talk about the history of the humble bond. I guess you talk about trying to pare things down to core themes. Here's the kind of two core themes that leaped out to me in the book. Number one was that a well structured and functioning bond market can essentially turn borrowing into a source of strength.
turns.zh: 好，那我们就来聊聊这只不起眼债券的历史。你谈到过要努力把事情精简到核心主题。书里有两个核心主题让我印象特别深刻。第一，一个结构良好、运转顺畅的债券市场，本质上能把借贷变成一种力量之源。

turns.en: It allows the issuer to prosecute wars, finance, infrastructure, all the things you need to build and maintain power. That was number one for me. And number two was that this proper functioning is really what you call the technology of how the debt works.
turns.zh: 它让发行方能够发动战争、为基础设施融资，也就是打造和维持权力所需的一切。这是第一点。第二点是，这种正常运转其实取决于你所说的'债务如何运作的技术'（technology of how the debt works）。

turns.en: That advances in power are often linked with changes in the how the bond. The technology of the bond works. Those are the two themes that really, I thought, leapt out to me. And I thought maybe we could use some stories from your book to illustrate those ideas. So perhaps we could begin with, begin at the beginning.
turns.zh: 权力的进阶往往与债券——债券运作技术——的变化相关联。这就是我认为真正跃然纸上的两个主题。我想我们也许可以用你书里的一些故事来阐释这些理念。那我们就从头开始讲起吧。

turns.en: Venice. Can you tell us how the Venetians came to develop a bond market and the role that that kind of played in supporting their rise as a power?
turns.zh: 威尼斯（Venice）。你能讲讲威尼斯人是怎么发展出债券市场的吗？以及这在支撑他们崛起为一个强权的过程中扮演了怎样的角色？

turns.en: I mean, by complete accident, I mean, in fact, they lost the war and that's how it was born, almost. So Venice was the rise in commercial power in the 12th century in the Mediterranean. It was kind of the perfect bridge between east and West. They were a republic at the time of everything else in Europe was an autocracy. They technically were ruled by Constantinople, the Byzantine Empire in Constantinople today Istanbul. But they were a Catholic Christian countries, so they also owed some
turns.zh: 完全是出于偶然——事实上，他们打输了那场战争，债券市场几乎就是这么诞生的。威尼斯是 12 世纪地中海崛起的商业强权，堪称东西方之间完美的桥梁。当时欧洲其他地方都是专制政体，而它是一个共和国。名义上它受君士坦丁堡（Constantinople）统治，也就是位于今天伊斯坦布尔的拜占庭帝国。但它是个天主教基督教地区，所以它也对——

turns.en: fealty to Rome. But essentially they didn't care. They just traded with everybody. They traded with Christians, they traded with Muslims, they traded with north, the south. Commerce was their ultimate loyalty and that made them fabulously rich, but annoyed everybody else around them. And eventually Constantinople got so upset with its uppity, not quite colony, but their uppity vassal state that they essentially decided to imprison every Venetian in Constantinople and the Byzantine Empire. And in this
turns.zh: ——罗马负有某种效忠义务。但本质上他们根本不在乎，他们跟所有人做贸易：跟基督徒做，跟穆斯林做，跟北方、南方都做。商业才是他们最终的忠诚，这让他们富得流油，却也惹恼了周围的所有人。最终君士坦丁堡对这个目中无人的、算不上殖民地、只能说是桀骜不驯的附庸国忍无可忍，于是决定把君士坦丁堡和拜占庭帝国境内的每一个威尼斯人都关起来。在这场——

turns.en: huge, actually incredibly impressive one day raid, we're talking tens of thousands of people and they didn't leak out, which must have been astonishing back in those days. But Venice decided, well, we need to teach our suzerain a lesson then. So they were going to sail a fleet and get their revenge and free their citizens.
turns.zh: ——规模庞大、其实令人惊叹的一日突击行动中，涉及数万人，而且消息竟然没有走漏，在那个年代一定相当惊人。但威尼斯决定：好，那我们得给宗主国一个教训。于是他们要派出一支舰队去复仇、去解救自己的公民。

turns.en: But they needed money to do so because back in the day those states were tiny. Like the state itself was small. Venice was rich, its people were rich, but the state itself was tiny. So they always borrowed money from the money lenders, the banks that were starting to crop up in Italy around then. But this required a far greater sum than you can just hit up a few banks for. So they essentially
turns.zh: 但他们需要钱才能办到，因为在那个年代，国家本身都很小。威尼斯很富，它的人民很富，但国家本身却很小。所以他们总是向放贷者、向当时开始在意大利冒头的那些银行借钱。但这次所需的金额远超你能随便找几家银行借到的数目。于是他们基本上——

turns.en: force all Venetians to pay a war tax, a one off war tax to the government that was proportional to their wealth. They assessed the wealth of everybody in the city and made everybody pay it. But to kind of soften the blow, they said, well, we're going to pay you 5% a year until we can repay this loan, this forced war loan slash tax. And look, if you're hard up for money, if you happen to need cash, we're going to make it traded. We're going to keep receipts of every loan that people made us. And
turns.zh: ——强制所有威尼斯人向政府缴纳一笔战争税，一次性的、与其财富成比例的战争贷款／税。他们评估了城里每个人的财富，让所有人都缴。但为了缓和冲击，他们说：好，在我们能偿还这笔贷款——这笔强制性战争贷款／税——之前，我们每年付你 5% 的利息。而且，如果你手头紧、正好需要现金，我们会让它可交易。我们会为每一笔借给我们的贷款保留收据。而——

turns.en: you can trade those receipts. Essentially you have to go down to the finance ministry and say, I've sold X amount of this prestiti
turns.zh: ——你可以交易这些收据。基本上你得去财政部说：我把一定数额的这种'prestiti'（强制性公债）卖掉了，

turns.en: from,. I. Don't know, Paolo to Luigi. And that was okay. And they built this massive fleet, sailed to Constantinople, but prevaricated, was struck down by the plague and had to return, for want of a better phrase, with her ass between the, the tail between their, I mean it was embarrassing. And also even worse, they brought the play back to Venice. So the doge, because it's a republic, he had to Defend this in front of all his citizens. He was summoned there and he was trying to explain. And the crowd was getting
turns.zh: ——比如从我叫不上名的 Paolo 卖给了 Luigi，这是被允许的。他们建起了这支庞大的舰队，驶向君士坦丁堡，却犹豫不决，又遭瘟疫袭击，只能——说得文雅点——夹着尾巴灰溜溜地回来，真是丢人。更糟的是，他们把瘟疫带回了威尼斯。所以那位总督（doge），因为这是个共和国，他必须当着全体公民的面为此辩护。他被传唤到场，试图解释，而人群变得越来越——

turns.en: angrier and angrier. And in the end all these advisors just very quietly tiptoed out. And eventually somebody started to attack the doge. He ran, he fled, but was beaten to death and stabbed on the streets of Venice, murdered for, for, for mismanaging this war. But of course, Venice couldn't pay that loan now that war tax. So it just became permanent. But it proved magic.
turns.zh: ——愤怒。到最后，那些顾问都悄悄溜了出去。终于有人开始攻击总督。他逃跑、他逃亡，但还是被殴打致死、被捅死在威尼斯街头，因为把这场战争搞砸而遭谋杀。当然，威尼斯现在无力偿还那笔贷款、那笔战争税了，于是它干脆变成了永久性的。但它证明有魔力。

turns.en: Suddenly people had something that they could buy, an income stream they could endow, give their daughters a dowry in the form of this. You could use it as collateral for trade. For the Venetians, that was particularly powerful. So suddenly in Venice's misfor, an incredibly powerful financial tool was made. And the, the core things was that it had a fixed interest rate that was key because it gave them sort of assurity. You were buying this and this would pay you X ducats a month, for example, or a
turns.zh: 突然间，人们有了一样可以购买的东西，一条可以传下去的收入流，可以用它给女儿做嫁妆，还可以拿它当贸易的抵押品。对威尼斯人来说，这一点尤其强大。于是，在威尼斯的这场不幸之中，一件极其强大的金融工具被创造了出来。而核心在于它有固定的利率，这一点很关键，因为它给了人们某种确定性：你买了它，它每个月（或每年）会付给你若干达克特（ducats），

turns.en: year, it was twice a yearly it was paid and that you could trade it. It was designed to be tradable and it wasn't a bearer bond. You had to register new buyers and sellers. But it was fairly easy to go down to the Rialto in Venice. It's still there. It's a, a fresh food market now. But that was the world's first bond market.
turns.zh: ——它一年付两次，而且你可以交易它。它被设计成可交易的，而且它不是无记名债券（bearer bond），新的买卖双方都得登记。不过去威尼斯的里亚托（Rialto）相当方便，它现在还在，如今是个生鲜食品市场。但那就是世界上第一个债券市场。

turns.en: And then you just bought and sold stuff and you'd wander over to the nearby finance ministry and just register the new owner, essentially. And it was such a great thing that the Italian city states copied it and it just spread out from there.
turns.zh: 然后你就在那买卖东西，再溜达到旁边的财政部去登记新的持有人，基本就是这样。这东西太棒了，意大利的各个城邦都争相效仿，它就这样传播开来。

turns.en: It seemed to me that the key to the success was the absolute, or I guess two things. One, that seemed that this kind of absolute determination not to default, so that it became, you know, it may be not quite as good as gold, but pretty close. And secondly, that the bondholders were also citizens. So they had a stake in the whole system.
turns.zh: 在我看来，成功的关键是那种绝对的——或者说有两点。第一，那种绝对不违约的决心，使它变得，你知道，也许不如黄金那么硬，但已经很接近了。第二，债券持有人同时也是公民，所以他们在整个体系里有切身利益。

turns.en: Yes. So they never default. They did default many hundred years later, but essentially they never fully repaid it. They would pay it down because Venice rose again and in fact did get revenge on Constantinople. They seized Constantinople 20, 30 years later, I think, and actually seized four beautiful bronze horses, Greek era horses from Constantinople stood on the hippodrome in Constantinople and you can still see them today in the cathedral there. And
turns.zh: 对。所以他们从不违约。几百年后他们确实违约过一次，但基本上他们从没全额偿还过。他们会逐步偿还，因为威尼斯再度崛起，事实上还真向君士坦丁堡报了仇。我记得大约二三十年后，他们攻占了君士坦丁堡，还夺走了四匹漂亮的青铜马——希腊时代的马，原本立在君士坦丁堡的赛马场（hippodrome）上，今天你在那座教堂里还能看到它们。而且——

turns.en: so they were able to use this as sort of almost like rocket fuel for the economy. I mean, Greece, it kind of, in a world where like, there's no digital money, it's just specie and trade actually Having something that kind of looks, walks, quacks and talks a bit like money is incredibly powerful for a merchant city. But it is also particularly powerful because it kind of entrenched democracy, because it gave citizens who owned this a vested interest in the proper governance of their own city
turns.zh: ——他们能把它当作经济几乎像火箭燃料一样的东西来用。在一个没有数字货币、只有铸币（specie）和贸易的世界里，拥有一样看起来、走起来、叫起来、说起话来都有点像货币的东西，对一个商业城邦来说极其强大。但它之所以特别强大，还因为它巩固了民主，因为它让持有它的公民对自己城邦的良善治理有了切身利益。

turns.en: state. So Venice, also the republic, the democracy of it, I mean imperfect by today's standards, but revolutionary for the era, became entrenched. And also they started publishing transparent state finances. They actually published what the government was spending and taking in. And in a world of autocracy, this was a little island of accountable quasi democracy. And it kind of shows that bonds can have multiple facets to them and can actually sometimes have positive unintended consequences
turns.zh: 所以威尼斯——这个共和国、这种民主，尽管以今天的标准看不完美，但在那个时代是革命性的——得到了巩固。而且他们开始公布透明的国家财政，真的把政府的支出和收入都公开了出来。在一个专制的世界里，这是一座负责任、准民主的小岛。这在某种程度上说明，债券可以有多重面向，有时甚至会带来正面的意外后果，

turns.en: as well. Not least making its citizens creditors citizens essentially and binding them even more closely together.
turns.zh: ——尤其是把它的公民变成了债权人公民，从而把他们更紧密地绑定在一起。

turns.en: Yeah, I thought that was just such a great example of like you say, borrowing, I suppose, has a negative connotation, but this was a great example of how it was in some sense an asset to the Venetian Republic. And later on there was another kind of technological change that I think was like 1262 or something, where they consolidated all these different issues into a single series. And that's something that we kind of see repeated throughout history and is very important. Can you explain why that consolidation was
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这真是个绝佳的例子。就像你说的，借贷大概带着负面的含义，但这个例子很好地说明了它在某种意义上其实是威尼斯共和国的一项资产。后来还有一次技术层面的变化，我记得大概是 1262 年前后，他们把所有这些不同的债券合并成了一个单一序列。这种事情在历史上反复出现，非常重要。你能解释一下，为什么那次合并是——

turns.en: a such an important kind of event? It was again, sort of emergencies. It's generally emergencies that push this forward. But they've been issuing happenstance, new loans, new war taxes here and there. And then they kind of realized, well, actually it's easy if we just consolidate this into a monte, literally a mountain of state debt. But despite the negative connotations that a mountain of debt sounds, having one homogenous pool of debt is even more powerful because first
turns.zh: ——如此重要的一件事？这又是出于紧急状况。一般来说，正是紧急状况推动了这些进步。他们此前到处临时发行新贷款、新战争税，然后他们意识到：其实只要把这些合并进一个 monte（字面意思就是'一座国家债务之山'）就省事多了。但尽管'一座债务之山'听起来有负面含义，拥有一个同质化的债务池其实更强大，因为首先——

turns.en: of all, it makes it far more easy to trade. You're not worried, am I buying this bond or that bond? What's better or worse? It just makes it far easier. And you can kind of see the contours of what the bond market is going to be. It's like freely tradable, homogenous and a fixed interest rate. The Venetians, because this was actually quite an incredible invention, they wouldn't let non Venetians buy, or only very rarely. It was an honor they bestowed on certain foreign were allowed to buy Venetian bonds.
turns.zh: ——它让交易容易得多。你不用担心'我该买这只还是那只债券？哪只更好哪只更差？'它就是让一切简单多了。你也能看出债券市场未来形态的轮廓：自由交易、同质化、固定利率。威尼斯人——因为这实际上是一项相当了不起的发明——不允许非威尼斯人购买，或者只是极少数情况下才允许。能被允许购买威尼斯债券，是他们赐予某些外国人的一种荣誉。

turns.en: So still fairly a very city centric bond market. And then each Italian city state just basically copied and pasted it. But you could see that sort of they taking the basic idea and starting to evolve, like improve on the technology gradually. And that's what we've seen Ever since.
turns.zh: 所以它仍然是一个非常以城邦为中心的债券市场。然后每个意大利城邦基本上就是复制粘贴。但你能看到他们在采纳这个基本理念后，开始逐步演化、逐步改进这项技术。而这正是我们此后一直看到的。

turns.en: Yeah, and that's actually a good unplanned, but good segue into my next kind of question, which was going to leap forward a few hundred years to talk about the uk. I believe you describe the UK bond market as eventually becoming the first reserve asset, which implies that a leap forward was creating a bond market where it could serve as stores of value for, for non citizens.
turns.zh: 是啊，这其实是个 unplanned 但却很好的过渡，正好引出我的下一个问题——我本打算向前跳几百年，聊聊英国（UK）。我记得你把英国债券市场描述为最终成为第一种储备资产（reserve asset），这意味着那次飞跃在于创造出一个债券市场，让它能够为非公民充当价值储藏手段。

turns.en: So I thought maybe you could explain the UK experience with the birth of, as you say, bonds is the first kind of reserve asset.
turns.zh: 所以我想，也许你能讲讲英国的这段经历——用你的话说，债券作为第一种储备资产的诞生。

turns.en: Well, it started with what the UK calls the Glorious revolution, though it was not considered glorious or revolution at the time.
turns.zh: 嗯，它始于英国人所说的光荣革命（Glorious Revolution），尽管在当时它并不被认为既光荣、也算不上革命。

turns.en: So the Dutch probably took the Italian invention of a bond market
turns.zh: 荷兰人大概采纳了意大利人发明的债券市场，

turns.en: and improved it the most. They created the first true bond market with different states, different towns, different water utilities, water boards, companies. The VOC issued the first corporate bond in the 1600s and they really kind of showed the power of it, but it was very Balkanized, it was not homogenous.
turns.zh: 并把它改进得最多。他们创造了第一个真正的债券市场，有各个州、各个城镇、各家水务公司、水利董事会、企业参与。VOC（荷兰东印度公司）在 1600 年代发行了第一只公司债券，他们真的展示了它的威力，但那个市场非常碎片化（Balkanized），并不同质。

turns.en: But they did sell bonds freely tradable. And they sold it to Brits, to Germans, to Belgians, to the French, to everybody. But it was mostly the Dutch. They were very thrifty, they're very saved. And they invested in bonds and used bonds to frankly managed to beat down this hyper power of the area, the Spanish Empire, and gain independence after a fairly sort of destructive hundred year war. The Brits kind of felt they'd kind of fallen behind
turns.zh: 但他们确实发行了可自由交易的债券，卖给了英国人、德国人、比利时人、法国人，卖给所有人。不过主要还是荷兰人自己买。他们非常节俭、非常能存钱，他们投资于债券，并借助债券，坦率说，成功击败了这个地区的超级强权——西班牙帝国，在一场相当具有破坏性的百年战争之后赢得了独立。英国人则觉得自己某种程度上落到了——

turns.en: another Protestant country, the Dutch. And this is time of huge religious tumult. The Dutch famously sailed in and raised the Royal Ship shipyard in England. So it was this sense that the Dutch, this tiny country that wasn't even a country until recently, have surpassed us. So a lot of the elite in England, basically, I mean, I use the phrase copy and paste, but that's what they did. They imported a Dutch prince and copied over a lot of Dutch financial practices and ideas. So that's led to the birth
turns.zh: ——另一个新教国家、也就是荷兰的后面。那是宗教剧烈动荡的时代。荷兰人曾经著名地突袭并摧毁了英国的皇家造船厂（Royal Ship shipyard）。于是就有这样一种感觉：荷兰这个直到最近都还算不上一个国家的弹丸小国，竟然超越了我们。所以英国很多精英基本上——我是说，我用了'复制粘贴'这个词，但他们干的就是这个。他们引进了一位荷兰亲王，把很多荷兰的金融做法和理念照搬了过来。这就导致了——

turns.en: of the bank of England, for example. It was still a state chartered but private bank then, but they also started moving towards a more consolidated holistic bond market. It took a long time, but eventually we saw the birth of something called consolidated annuities, because it was all these different annuities, as they were called, consolidated to one pool. And they used to pay 4 or 5% and you typically say they're going to pay 4%. And at times of war there were perpetual bonds. Countries always issued perpetual
turns.zh: ——比如英格兰银行（Bank of England）的诞生。它当时是一家由国家特许、但仍是私人的银行。他们也开始朝着一个更整合、更整体的债券市场迈进。这花了很长时间，但最终我们看到了一种叫做'统一年金'（consolidated annuities，即 Consols）的东西诞生，因为它把当时各种各样被称作年金的债券整合进了一个池子。它们过去通常付 4% 或 5%，你一般会说它们付 4%。战时则有永续债券（perpetual bonds）。当时各国总是发行永续——

turns.en: bonds back then. The interest rate didn't tend to change that much. They issued at 4%, 5%, but if demand wasn't Sufficient, they'd sell it at a discount. So you could buy, let's say a 4% consolidated annuity at 90 pence on the pound, if people are worried about the UK. And then when the UK was doing well, maybe that'd be trading at 110 pence. So now it's the real. Definitely, you can see today's bond market there. And the essential new thing was that, that
turns.zh: ——债券。利率往往变化不大，他们以 4%、5% 发行，但如果需求不足，就会打折出售。所以如果人们担心英国，你可以按每英镑 90 便士的价格买到一只 4% 的统一年金；而当英国表现好时，它也许会以 110 便士交易。所以这才是真正的——你绝对能从中看到今天的债券市场。而本质上的新东西在于——

turns.en: the Netherlands was a collection of lots of states and they were very mercantile. They were kind of. They'd taken over the great commercial, most commercial people in the world, probably then. But it wasn't one sovereign nation state in the same way England was. And in fact, that proved not just very attractive to Brits, but to the Dutch. The Dutch bankroll the UK to a huge extent. You know, there's a reason why even the Americans during the Revolutionary War, they went to the Netherlands to ask for
turns.zh: ——荷兰是许多州的集合体，而且非常商业化。他们大概成了当时世界上最善于经商的民族。但它并不像英国那样是一个单一的主权民族国家。而事实上，这一点不仅对英国人很有吸引力，对荷兰人也是。荷兰在很大程度上为英国提供资金支持。你知道，就连美国人在独立战争期间都跑去荷兰求——

turns.en: loans. They were so the bankers to the world and English took advantage of it. But that's kind of. I'd say the first bond is that Prestiti in Venice. But there are people that say the true birth of the bond market is actually in the 1600s in Britain. And then you can decide whether is it the birth of the bank of England and it's the bond that it backed, or is it some of the later issues like the consolidated annuities? But it was, I think, the Brits that really showed how you build a national
turns.zh: ——贷款，他们就是这么一群'世界的银行家'，而英国人利用了这一点。不过我想说，最早的债券是威尼斯那种 Prestiti。但也有人认为，债券市场真正的诞生其实是在 1600 年代的英国。然后你可以自己判断，究竟是英格兰银行的诞生及其所支持的债券，还是后来的一些发行、比如统一年金。但我认为，正是英国人真正展示了如何建立一个国家级的——

turns.en: sovereign bond market and the power that that can give you. And what was it about the consoles that allowed them to serve as a reserve asset?
turns.zh: 主权债券市场，以及它能带给你怎样的力量。那么，Consols 究竟有什么特质，使它得以充当一种储备资产呢？

turns.en: Well, that didn't start immediately, though foreigners did buy them. But it's because, partially because of the Glorious Revolution, also lessened the power of the royals. So back in the day, if you lent money to Spain, really what you were doing, you were lending money to the Spanish king. And push comes to shove, the king can chop your head off. So lending to autocrats is always a bit dicey. But in England, it started shifting out of the royal family and Parliament took more and more control of the purse
turns.zh: 嗯，这并非一开始就实现的，尽管外国人确实买了它们。但部分原因在于，光荣革命也削弱了王室的权力。在过去，如果你借钱给西班牙，你实际上是在借钱给西班牙国王。而一旦闹翻，国王可以砍掉你的脑袋。所以借钱给专制君主总是有点冒险。但在英国，权力开始从王室手中转移出去，议会对钱袋子的控制越来越——

turns.en: strings. So it was Parliament that was issuing these bonds, England as a country, not whatever family was sitting on the throne at that point. And they also started again, a bit like the Italians publishing more transparent state finances and the fact that the Parliament could keep the king in check. The word checks and balances, actually, it's incredible reading what some Dutch merchants would say, why they started investing in Britain, because they just like that. And then over time, that bond market made
turns.zh: ——大。所以发行这些债券的是议会，是作为一个国家的英格兰，而不是当时坐在王位上的某个家族。他们也再次开始——有点像意大利人那样——公布更透明的国家财政，而且议会能够制衡国王。说到'制衡'（checks and balances）这个词，读一些荷兰商人写的、关于他们为什么开始投资英国的话，真是令人惊叹，因为他们就是喜欢这一点。而随着时间推移，那个债券市场让——

turns.en: Britain more powerful. One of the reasons, a large reason why England was able to beat Napoleon eventually wasn't. I mean, Horatio Nelson and the Duke of Wellington did an incredible job. But England was only able to fight for so long against a far larger enemy because it could fund itself to an enormous degree by the bond market. Even Napoleon marveled at how England could do this. So he called Britain a nation of shopkeepers, rather pejoratively.
turns.zh: ——英国变得更强大。英格兰最终能打败拿破仑的一个、也是很大一个原因——我是说，Horatio Nelson 和 Wellington 公爵立下了非凡战功，但英格兰之所以能对一个强大得多的敌人作战这么久，是因为它能在极大程度上通过债券市场为自己融资。连拿破仑都惊叹英格兰是怎么做到的。所以他略带贬义地称英国为一个'店主之国'（a nation of shopkeepers）。

turns.en: But it was then afterwards you can see that England was triumphant and the British bond market was huge. But because people trusted England to keep paying those bonds, they never defaulted. They just became kind of portable money in an era where, yeah, again, gold and silver sometimes were in short supply. So it just became something that was valuable. And if England or English merchants wanted to buy something, a lot of people around the world, certainly in Europe would accept consoles as payment. And that's,
turns.zh: 但在那之后你能看到，英格兰大获全胜，英国债券市场规模庞大。因为人们相信英格兰会持续偿付这些债券，它们从不违约，于是它们就成了一种'便携的货币'——在那个金银有时短缺的时代，对，它就成了有价值的东西。如果英格兰或英国商人想买点什么，世界上很多人、至少在欧洲，都愿意接受 Consols 作为支付手段。而这——

turns.en: you know, the word guild is the Dutch bonds that was considered super safe, issued by the Holland, for example, the strongest province. So there have been some quasi safe currency. So reserve currencies before the Roman denarius has cropped up all the way in China and India. We've found hordes of Roman silver coins showing that both those are current accounts deficit with Asia, but also that they did accept Roman coins. But I think in the sort of semi modern era, the great British bond market, the consul market
turns.zh: ——你知道，'guild'这个词指的是荷兰债券，被视为超级安全，比如由最强的省份 Holland 发行。所以在罗马第纳尔（denarius）之前就有过一些准安全货币、储备货币，罗马银币一路在中国和印度出现过。我们发现过成批的罗马银币，既显示当时对亚洲存在经常账户赤字，也说明他们确实接受罗马硬币。但我认为，在半现代时期，伟大的英国债券市场、也就是 Consols 市场——

turns.en: is the OUD treasury market. Essentially it was for several hundred years.
turns.zh: ——就相当于如今的美国国债市场。本质上，它在几百年里都是如此。

turns.en: It's an interesting through line, isn't it? Because Venice, then the Dutch Republic and then the uk, they were all kind of early forms of democracy and the bond markets developed sequentially in those states. And that doesn't seem to be an accident. It seems like there has to be some sort of, I don't know, external disciplinary mechanism to give the bond market or give the investors some sense of that they're not just that they're going to get repaid.
turns.zh: 这是条很有意思的主线，不是吗？因为威尼斯、然后是荷兰共和国、再然后是英国，它们都是某种早期形式的民主政体，而债券市场正是在这些国家里相继发展起来的。这看起来并非巧合。似乎必须有某种——我不知道——外部的约束机制，来让债券市场、让投资者有一种确信：他们终将得到偿还。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, it's, I mean the true aspects of this one, which actually surprised me when I was doing research for this one, which I knew that broadly speaking, the countries that have been successful are the ones that have nurtured bond markets and have frankly embraced finance. I mean, finance, you know, is not very popular.
turns.zh: 是啊，这方面有个真相，其实是我在做研究时才发现并感到惊讶的：大体而言，那些成功的国家，都是培育了债券市场、并且坦率说拥抱了金融的国家。我是说，金融，你知道，并不是很受欢迎。

turns.en: It has never been popular. There's a reason why every single major religion has some prohibition against interests or usury. It still is today. It's not popular. But broadly speaking, the more financially sophisticated a country and economy is, the better it has done. It has better been able to mobilize the wealth of its citizens to reinforce that progress essentially.
turns.zh: 它从来都不受欢迎。每一个主要宗教都对利息或高利贷（usury）有某种禁令，这绝非偶然。直到今天也是如此，它就是不受待见。但大体而言，一个国家和经济体在金融上越成熟，它表现得就越好，就越能调动本国公民的财富来巩固那种进步，本质上就是这样。

turns.en: And the Bond market is a great example of it. So I knew even before I wrote the book that I was very confident that as I was studying this more and more, that strong bond markets lead to stronger countries and stronger countries lead to stronger bond markets.
turns.zh: 债券市场就是一个绝佳的例子。所以早在写这本书之前，随着我研究得越来越深入，我就非常确信：强大的债券市场造就更强大的国家，而更强大的国家又造就更强大的债券市场。

turns.en: And it's a positive feedback loop. The one thing that surprised me, which goes back to the citizen credited citizen aspect in Venice, is that to what extent actually the bond market helped entrench and spread democracy in Europe. And it goes back to again, England, because people felt more comfortable lending money to England because it was a democracy, because it had representative democracy and it controlled the powers of the king. But the parliament was also controlled. There were checks and balances and that
turns.zh: 这是一个正反馈循环。有一件事让我惊讶——这又回到威尼斯那种'公民即债权人'的层面——那就是债券市场在多大程度上实际上帮助巩固并在欧洲传播了民主。这又回到英国：人们更愿意把钱借给英国，因为它是一个民主政体，因为它有代议制民主、它约束了国王的权力，但议会也同样受到约束，存在制衡。而这——

turns.en: was why people felt. And then London and England could borrow more cheaply. And that again strengthened its advantages when other countries realized that they too also implemented, at the very least, certain democratic reforms, certain transparency measures.
turns.zh: ——正是人们如此感受的原因。于是伦敦和英国就能以更低的成本借钱，当其他国家意识到这一点后，这又进一步放大了它的优势，它们也——至少——推行了某些民主改革、某些透明度措施。

turns.en: And the most most obvious way of seeing this is Prussia. So that the precursor to modern Germany after the Napoleonic wars went to Nathan Meyer Rothschild, or the Rothschild family in London that was emerging as the big of the bond kings of the era, and said, we want to issue a bond in England. And Rothschild said, well, sure, you can do that, but you have to do it in pounds.
turns.zh: 最明显的例子就是普鲁士（Prussia）。拿破仑战争之后，这个现代德国的前身去找 Nathan Meyer Rothschild，或者说去找伦敦的 Rothschild 家族——他们当时正崛起为那个时代的债券之王——说：我们想在英国发行一只债券。Rothschild 说：好，当然可以，但你们必须以英镑计价发行。

turns.en: And British investors will want to see you control the power of the King of Prussia and publish some numbers. You'll have to do these things. And there's letters. Neil Ferguson, the historian, has written fantastically about this. And it's quite remarkable seeing how supremely wealthy but still a Jewish family in an era of rampant prejudice in Europe is writing letters to the finance minister of Prussia saying, just forget it, son.
turns.zh: 而且英国投资者会希望看到你们约束普鲁士国王的权力，并公布一些数字。你们必须做这些事。相关信件还留存着。历史学家 Niall Ferguson 就此写过极其精彩的内容。看到这样一个极其富有、但在那个欧洲偏见横行的时代仍是犹太人的家族，写信给普鲁士财政部长说'别想了，小子'，实在令人称奇。

turns.en: You aren't going to get this money unless you do exactly what I tell you. And Prussia did commit. I mean, they kind of backtracked on a few things, but again, you can see that you start seeing it kind of them moving in the right direction. And I don't think the bond markets have helped democracy flourish or anything like that, but it was kind of on the side of the angels, one might say, and was a reinforcing factor in that general push away from autocratic royal families that we saw around that.
turns.zh: '除非你完全照我说的做，否则别想拿到这笔钱。'而普鲁士确实做出了承诺。我是说，他们在几件事上有点反悔，但你还是能看到他们开始朝正确的方向移动。我不认为债券市场促成了民主的繁荣之类的，但可以说它站在了天使的一边，是我们当时看到的那股 overall 摆脱专制王室家族的推力中的一个强化因素。

turns.en: This is going to take us a little bit off piece. But before we move from Europe to the US I wanted to ask, as I was reading this section talking about how both Venice and then the UK had big leaps forward when they consolidated their various bond issues into a single issue, I started thinking about the current state of Europe and how it seemed to me a little ironic that the birth of the modern bond market was in Europe and was turbocharged by a consolidation of individual state debts. And that's really what
turns.zh: 这会让我们稍微跑题一点。但在我们从欧洲转到美国之前，我想问一下：读这部分讲到威尼斯、然后英国都在把各自的多种债券发行合并成单一发行时实现了大飞跃，我开始思考欧洲当前的状况，我觉得有点讽刺的是，现代债券市场诞生于欧洲，并且是靠合并各个国家的债务而被强力助推的。而这其实正是——

turns.en: you're looking at a situation now in the eu. And I don't know, do you, do you have, do you see that parallel and do you, do you kind of see there's any chance that maybe that they'll kind of learn, relearn the lesson of history and have some type of consolidated debt that, you know, might turbocharge the, I don't know, power of the European Union?
turns.zh: ——你如今在欧盟（EU）看到的局面。我不知道，你会不会看到这个类比？你觉得有没有可能他们会重新学习历史的教训，搞出某种合并债务，从而——你知道——强力助推欧盟的实力？

turns.en: Yes and no. I mean, to deal with the consolidated debts, I do not think we're ever going to see that. Unfortunately, in that true sense of the way people talk about euro bonds, European government supranational bonds, we have it a little bit in bonds issued by the EU and the European Investment bank and the European Stability Mechanism that kind of are kind of, I mean, I'd say they are eurobonds, they are jointly guaranteed and they are the responsibility of the taxpayers across the region. But
turns.zh: 既是也不是。就合并债务而言，我不认为我们会看到那种东西。遗憾的是，在人们谈论欧元债券（euro bonds）那种真正的意义上——欧洲政府的超国家债券——我们确实有一点：欧盟、欧洲投资银行（European Investment Bank）和欧洲稳定机制（European Stability Mechanism）发行的债券就有点那个意思。我是说，我会称它们为欧元债券，它们由各方共同担保，是整个地区纳税人的责任。但——

turns.en: in the sort of total sense where they issue European Treasuries and it's the birth of the European treasury market essentially in euros, I think that the sense of nationhood is a little bit too entrenched for it's essentially, it's always, you can see this in the US where the US was at 1 point a creditor nation, like every country in the world owed the US money and that obviously informed how the US thought about things. Now, of course, the US is a debtor country, it thinks completely different about
turns.zh: ——在那种完全的意义上，也就是发行欧洲国债、本质上以欧元计价的欧洲国债市场诞生，我认为那种民族国家认同感根深蒂固得有点过头了。本质上一直是这样，你可以在美国看到：美国一度是个债权国，世界上每个国家都欠美国的钱，那显然影响了美国对事物的思考方式。而现在，美国当然是个债务国，它对这些事情的看法完全不同了。

turns.en: these things. And then Europe, you know, maybe at some point the south has a renaissance and the north goes down, you know, but broadly speaking, there's always going to be somebody nobody wants to essentially be seen or seen to be sort of bailing out their neighbors, as it were. So I sad, I think it would be a great thing, but I think the Europe can get a little bit way there. And I would say that I'm way more optimistic than I was about some of these, than before. I mean, I covered the Eurozone crisis, I
turns.zh: 至于欧洲，你知道，也许某个时候南方复兴、北方衰落，但大体而言，总归会有一些人——没有人愿意被人看到、或被认为在救助自己的邻居，可以说是这样。所以我说，我觉得那会是件好事，但我认为欧洲能朝那个方向走一点。而且我得说，比起以前，我对这些事情乐观多了。我是说，我报道过欧元区危机，也——

turns.en: covered the financial crisis and, and if I'd gone back 10 years ago, the idea that European policymakers would be talking gushingly about capital markets and securitization and joint financial regulation, all these things, I mean it would have been unthinkable.
turns.zh: ——报道过金融危机。如果回到 10 年前，说欧洲的政策制定者会热情洋溢地谈论资本市场、证券化（securitization）和联合金融监管这一切，那简直是不可想象的。

turns.en: I mean, obviously they had a bond market, it was a sovereign market. The corporate bond market was not meaningful. The high yield market was almost non existent and it was seen as this is an emblem of American style capitalism. That was broken by 2008, but now, I mean, Europe would kill for a smidgen of what the US has. It's kind of been realized that this is at the very least a good adjunct to your banking system, but actually might be even superior. And I think it's going to move very slowly, but I
turns.zh: 我是说，他们显然有债券市场，那是个主权债券市场。公司债券市场无足轻重，高收益（high yield）市场几乎不存在，而且这被视为美式资本主义的标志——那套东西在 2008 年被打破了。但现在，欧洲哪怕能得到美国所拥有的一丁点都求之不得。人们已经意识到，这至少是你银行体系的一个很好的补充，甚至可能更优越。我认为它会推进得非常缓慢，但我——

turns.en: feel for the first time across political sort of sides, across different countries, there is general broad agreement on the direction of travel. And, you know, it's a bit like a supertanker. It's like a fleet of supertankers. It's going to take a while to get where you want them to go, but they're going there now. So I'm actually more optimistic on the direction, if not the speed, than I've been for a very long time.
turns.zh: ——第一次感觉到，跨越政治阵营、跨越不同国家，大家在前进方向上有了普遍而广泛的共识。你知道，这有点像一艘超级油轮，或者说一支超级油轮船队，要开到你想去的地方得花上一阵子，但它们现在正朝那儿开。所以其实我对方向更乐观，即便对速度不那么乐观。

turns.en: I think maybe this is a good point. We can actually talk more about the modern bond market and which really, where Europe is involved with the kind of birth of what's called, often confusingly, the Euro bond market. Can you. Since that really. I think you do point to that as the beginning of the modern bond market. Can you kind of just walk us through what happened there, why they're called Euro bonds and why it's so important for financial centers to have good restaurants?
turns.zh: 我觉得也许这是个很好的切入点，可以更多地聊聊现代债券市场，尤其是欧洲与所谓——常常令人混淆的——欧洲债券（Eurobond）市场诞生的那段渊源。既然你确实把那个当作现代债券市场的开端，你能不能给我们梳理一下当时发生了什么、为什么它们叫 Eurobond，以及为什么对金融中心来说拥有好的餐厅如此重要？

turns.en: Yes. So these are kind of the original Eurobonds. So after World War II, I mean, Europe was in tatters. I think we almost forget it was within living memory of at least our parents. And it's hard to exaggerate how bad things were. And the US In a major way, stepped up to the plate, pumped money through the martial aid. Eventually the World bank also came playing in. The imf, helped budget the system, the whole Bretton woods system, essentially.
turns.zh: 是的。这些才算是最初的欧洲债券（Eurobonds）。二战之后，欧洲一片废墟。我想我们几乎忘了，那至少还在我们父辈的记忆所及之内。当时情况有多糟，怎么形容都不为过。美国大力站了出来，通过马歇尔援助（Marshall aid）注入资金。最终世界银行（World Bank）也参与进来，国际货币基金组织（IMF）帮助搭建了这套体系——本质上就是整个布雷顿森林体系。

turns.en: So Europe did recover, but it meant that the US went from being this massive credit nation, every country owed them money, to more and more dollars seeping out into the world. That's a great thing. The dollar was the only currency that was still pegged to gold, and other currencies were pegged to the dollar. So the dollar was kind of the world's gold. And this is the birth of the American exorbitant privilege. But the position, the unique position
turns.zh: 欧洲确实复苏了，但这意味着美国从这样一个庞大的债权国——每个国家都欠它钱——变成了越来越多的美元渗透到世界各地。这是件好事。美元是唯一仍与黄金挂钩的货币，其他货币则与美元挂钩，所以美元有点像是'世界的黄金'。这就是美国'嚣张的特权'（exorbitant privilege）的诞生。但那种地位、那种独特的地位——

turns.en: in today's financial system, but it meant lots of dollars floating around the world because other people would use them as currency.
turns.zh: ——在当今金融体系中的地位——也意味着大量美元在世界各地流动，因为其他人会把它们当货币使用。

turns.en: Hilariously, this included Soviet banks in Eastern Europe or certainly sort of communist banks, banks owned by communist states like East Germany and Poland, but also the Soviet Union itself.
turns.zh: 好笑的是，这其中还包括东欧的苏联银行，或者至少说是共产主义性质的银行——由东德、波兰等共产主义国家拥有的银行，也包括苏联自己。

turns.en: And they, because they had to buy and sell stuff, they exported banks still do these things even in Communist countries. So they had all these dollars and they didn't want to keep them in the US they kept them in Europe. And there's a bank in, in Paris called B, said Bon Commercial is near east or something. I wrote something like that bsan and it had a lot of the Soviet Union's overseas dollars and it had the wire address Eurobank. So whenever it wide money to somebody who say Eurobank. So these dollars, offshore
turns.zh: 因为他们得买卖东西——即便在共产主义国家，银行也照样做这些进出口的事。所以他们手里有所有这些美元，却不想把它们留在美国，就存在了欧洲。巴黎有一家银行，叫 Banque Commerciale 什么的（转写不清），我写过类似'B-S-A-N'的名字，它持有苏联大量的海外美元，而且它的电汇地址是 Eurobank。所以每当它给某人汇款时，就会显示 Eurobank。于是这些离岸的美元——

turns.en: dollars, were just called euro dollars. So offshore currencies are generally always called euro dollars, even if they're not actually euros or dollars or whatever. But you suddenly saw a huge pool with this. American companies were exporting and selling abroad.
turns.zh: ——就被叫做欧洲美元（euro dollars）。所以离岸货币通常都被叫做欧洲美元，即便它们其实并不是欧元或美元之类的。但你突然就看到一个巨大的资金池。美国公司当时在向海外出口和销售。

turns.en: They didn't always necessarily want to repatriate it to the US So you have all these dollars started hoard up elsewhere and people realize, well, this seems like an opportunity for a banker. And at the time, because London had been shattered by the war, the city of London, Europe in general, you'd see European companies and European states and European cities go to the US to borrow because the US was the only game in town. So that's the birth of the truth. And the Yankee market, I guess we'd call it now
turns.zh: 他们并不总是愿意把钱汇回美国，于是所有这些美元开始在别处囤积起来，人们意识到：嗯，这对银行家来说像是个机会。当时，因为伦敦被战争摧毁了——伦敦金融城、乃至整个欧洲——你会看到欧洲公司、欧洲国家、欧洲城市都跑去美国借钱，因为美国是唯一的选择。这就是'扬基市场'（Yankee market）的诞生，我想我们现在会这么称呼它，

turns.en: that foreign companies issuing dollar bonds in the U.S. the U.S. investment investors. But as Europe improved and ameliorated, European investors were buying stuff, especially in Switzerland for example. And you had this perverse situation where European companies would go to the US to borrow from European investors.
turns.zh: ——也就是外国公司在美国向美国投资者发行美元债券。但随着欧洲改善、好转，欧洲投资者开始买东西，比如在瑞士尤其如此。于是就出现了这种扭曲的局面：欧洲公司跑去美国，向欧洲投资者借钱。

turns.en: A lot of bankers, particularly in London, thought this was a travesty. So they decided to use those euro dollars to create the euro bond market. And it's just euro bonds and it's not necessarily European.
turns.zh: 很多银行家，尤其是伦敦的，认为这简直荒唐。所以他们决定用那些欧洲美元来创造欧洲债券（Eurobond）市场。它就是 Eurobond，而且并不一定是欧洲的。

turns.en: Lots of countries around the world issue. It's basically the bond market at its most borderless and international. And it kind of harnessed all those dormant pools of euro dollars that were kind of pooling around in bank accounts around the world and recreated I guess what Nathan Meyer Rothschild originally created a bond market. And it was essential to rebuilding London as a financial center for the world. From the 60s onwards, people would think of equities and stocks and the uk. There's almost legends about
turns.zh: 世界上很多国家都在发行。它基本上就是债券市场最无国界、最国际化的形态。它把那些沉睡在世界各银行账户里、四处积聚的欧洲美元资金池利用了起来，重新创造了我猜就是 Nathan Meyer Rothschild 最初创造的那种债券市场。这对把伦敦重建为世界金融中心至关重要。从 60 年代起，人们一提到英国的股票和股市，就几乎有关于——

turns.en: the big bang, the reforms that came under Margaret Thatcher. But the city's renaissance had started long before then. And it was built on the back of bonds as it had been in the 19th century as well.
turns.zh: ——'大爆炸'（Big Bang，即 Margaret Thatcher 时期的那些改革）的传奇。但伦敦金融城的复兴其实早在那之前就开始了。而它跟 19 世纪一样，是建立在债券之上的。

turns.en: And then I guess this became successful that enough that you know, US companies started selling them as well.
turns.zh: 然后我猜，这个市场成功到连美国公司也开始发行它们了。

turns.en: Well, yes, because I mean there was so much money abroad. Because also they don't forget in the US I mean you could almost write an entire book just on Regulation Q. Do you remember Regulation Q? I do, yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 嗯，是的，因为海外有太多钱了。另外别忘了在美国国内——我几乎可以单就 Q 条例（Regulation Q）写一整本书。你还记得 Q 条例吗？我记得，是的，没错。

turns.en: They restricted what savings and loans could restricted the interest rates they could pay. Is that right? Yeah. So deposit accounts this plain window weren't supposed to pay any interest and saving accounts were capped and they were set by government. And this was born in the Great Depression.
turns.zh: 它限制了储蓄贷款机构（savings and loans）能付的利率。是这样吗？对。所以活期存款账户本不该付任何利息，储蓄账户的利率则被设了上限，而且由政府设定。这诞生于大萧条（Great Depression）时期。

turns.en: And I think it made perfect sense then in the rebuilding of the World War. You don't want too much money hoarding. So it kind of is one of those things that makes perfect sense at the time. But over time it increasingly becomes perverse and silly and it kind of obviously repelled and forced a lot of encouraged people to keep money offshore because you could put the money into a Eurodollar account at HSBC or BNP Paribas Deutsche bank and make more than you could at JP Morgan. The US also had started swung from a massive
turns.zh: 我觉得在当时、在战后重建中，这完全说得通：你不希望有太多钱被囤积起来。所以它是那种在当时完全合理的东西。但随着时间推移，它变得越来越扭曲、越来越愚蠢，而且显然把很多人赶到了、或者说鼓励人们把钱留在离岸，因为你可以把钱存进汇丰（HSBC）、法国巴黎银行（BNP Paribas）或德意志银行（Deutsche Bank）的欧洲美元账户，赚得比存在摩根大通（JP Morgan）更多。美国自己也已从庞大的——

turns.en: current account surplus to a deficit. So the US was actually quite keen to keep dollars overseas as well. They encouraged this because it helped, helped keep the at least protect some value of the dollar as it was losing its value. But essentially USM companies eventually as well decided, well, you have this hugely vibrant dollar bond market and it's offshore, but we don't care where we borrow money.
turns.zh: ——经常账户顺差转向了逆差。所以美国其实也很乐意把美元留在海外。他们鼓励这样做，因为这有助于、至少能保护美元在贬值过程中的一部分价值。但本质上，美国公司最终也决定：好，你有一个极其活跃的离岸美元债券市场，可我们不在乎在哪儿借钱。

turns.en: We have operations abroad as well. So they started tapping it.
turns.zh: 我们在海外也有业务。于是他们开始去利用那个市场。

turns.en: Eventually developing countries started tapping it and it just became so old time is still call it the Eurobond market, but it is essentially the external bond markets, the big bad international bond market that is truly stateless. It is not just in London, it's everywhere. And it is, I mean, tens of trillions of dollars worth. It's hugely vibrant and fascinating. And you've got countries like the Vatican, Papua New Guinea, Russia though they're shut out now. The Church of England issued dollar
turns.zh: 最终发展中国家也开始利用它，它就变得如此——如今人们仍叫它欧洲债券市场，但它本质上就是外部债券市场，那个庞大、真正无国界的国际债券市场。它不只在伦敦，而是无处不在。它的规模有数万亿美元之巨，极其活跃、极其迷人。发行方有梵蒂冈（Vatican）、巴布亚新几内亚（Papua New Guinea）、俄罗斯（虽然现在被排除在外）。连英格兰教会（Church of England）都发行过美元——

turns.en: bonds. It's frankly wildly vibrant and impressive. Yeah. And I guess the other aspect that I really appreciated about your book, I mean these are historical stories, but there's also a lot of great individual characters in there and maybe we could talk about a couple of those. To me, the most interesting is Michael Milken. And partly because, you know, I wouldn't say he's forgotten exactly, but I mean, I think for people, certainly my generation, we haven't forgotten him, but I think the younger
turns.zh: ——债券。坦率说，它活跃得惊人、令人印象深刻。是啊。我想你书里另一个我很欣赏的方面是：这些虽然是历史故事，但里面也有很多精彩的个体人物，也许我们可以聊聊其中几位。对我来说最有意思的是 Michael Milken。部分原因是，你知道，我不会说他被完全遗忘了，但我认为，对我们这代人来说肯定没忘记他，可对更年轻的——

turns.en: generation, they really don't know who he is and how influential he was in creating, in helping create aspects of the modern barn market. So I was wondering maybe if we could just not bring him back to life because he's still alive. But I mean, let's talk a little bit about his role in the modern bond market. Can you tell us about his, his kind of original inspiration that he had at UC Berkeley and how that kind of set him off on his career?
turns.zh: ——一代人来说，他们真不知道他是谁、不知道他在帮助缔造现代债券市场某些方面上有多大影响力。所以我在想，也许我们可以——不是让他'复活'，因为他还在世——但我们可以稍微聊聊他在现代债券市场中的角色。你能讲讲他当初在 UC Berkeley 获得的灵感，以及那是如何开启他的职业生涯的吗？

turns.en: Yeah, I mean he's one of my favorites as well. He did not talk to me for the book. He refused to talk. But all the people are still alive and living. He's probably one of the people I would most have liked to talk to just because he is I think genuinely more fascinating and complex than maybe even the people I know him appreciate. Certainly even before me, he's just a very interesting guy. So yeah, he was at Berkeley and he's switched to business studies and he was very brainy. I mean this is a guy that
turns.zh: 是啊，他也是我最喜欢的人物之一。他没有为这本书接受我的采访，他拒绝谈。但在所有仍在世的人里，他大概是我最想与之交谈的人之一，只因为我觉得他确实比那些认识他、欣赏他的人所认为的还要更迷人、更复杂——当然也比我更甚。他就是一个非常有意思的人。所以，对，他在伯克利，转到了商科，而且非常聪明。我是说，这是个——

turns.en: I heard from other students that they didn't want to take his classes because they graded on the curve and you just know you're not going to get top grade. When he was in there, he was like the teachers would ask him questions, he was that smart. But at Berkeley stumbled over a book by a guy called Braddock Hickman who was then a little known academic who actually would go on to lead one of the regional feds. But Braddock Hickman had written an incredibly dense study of corporate defaults from I think the
turns.zh: ——我从别的同学那里听说，他们不想跟他同班上课，因为成绩按曲线（curve）评，你只要他在班里，就注定拿不到最高分。他就是那么聪明，聪明到连老师都会反过来问他问题。但在伯克利，他偶然读到了一本书，作者是一个叫 Braddock Hickman 的人——当时还是个默默无闻的学者，后来其实去领导了一家地区联邦储备银行。Braddock Hickman 写过一项极其艰深的研究，考察的是我认为从——

turns.en: turn of the early start of the 20th century to around the 1960s.
turns.zh: ——20 世纪初到大约 1960 年代期间的公司违约情况。

turns.en: And Henny showed that actually ratings are broadly accurate. The credit ratings, the higher the rating, the less chance of defaults and lowly rated credits. Corporate bonds did default more but and this was the sensational bit, the returns on those badly rated bonds were so much higher that even though they defaulted in greater numbers, your returns were vastly better. Better in junk bonds. And you obviously couched it in very sort of academic language. It's very, I've read that paper. It is
turns.zh: Hickman 证明，信用评级其实大体是准确的：评级越高，违约概率越低；而那些低评级的公司债确实违约更多。但——这才是最惊人的部分——那些低评级债券的回报率高得多，以至于即便它们违约的数量更多，你的回报依然要好得多，在高收益债券（junk bonds）上更好。当然，他是用非常学术化的语言来表述的。我读过那篇论文，它——

turns.en: not gripping, it's really interesting. It's really good data work at a time when frankly don't forget this kind of not quite pre computers but I don't think he had access to a computer. So it's impressive work but it is not written grippingly. But Mike Milken as a student immediately grasped it and that kind of became the zeitgeist like or his the whole thing that guided through life. They're like companies are unfairly rated not because like they don't default, but they just are paid too
turns.zh: ——并不引人入胜，但确实很有意思，是在那个年代——别忘了，那还不算完全是计算机出现之前，但我不认为他能用上计算机——做出的非常出色的数据工作。所以这是项了不起的成果，只是写得并不吸引人。但学生时代的 Mike Milken 立刻就抓住了它的精髓，那几乎成了他的时代信条、成了指引他一生的东西。也就是说：这些公司被不公平地评级了，不是因为它们不违约，而是它们被要求付太高的——

turns.en: much. They are shut out of markets. This is unfair. People should be lending more to these companies because you make more returns, but also you can open up access to capital to all sorts of companies. That might look bad, and some of them are bad and some of them will default. But broadly speaking, if you have a broad enough diversified basket, you'll make out like a banter it.
turns.zh: ——代价，它们被挡在市场之外。这不公平。人们本该更多地借钱给这些公司，因为你不仅能获得更高的回报，还能为各种各样的公司打开融资渠道。它们也许看上去不怎么样，其中有些确实很糟、有些会违约。但大体而言，只要你持有一个足够分散的组合，你就能赚得盆满钵满。

turns.en: And that was the cornerstone realization of what became a pretty incredible junk bond empire.
turns.zh: 而这，正是后来那个相当了不起的高收益债券帝国赖以建立的基石认知。

turns.en: Yeah, and you say, I mean the stories about Milken are really good. I mean, you say he had this five hour commute from Philadelphia to New York and he hired a guy to sit next to him so that no one would talk to him so that he could spend his time studying the bond market. I really appreciated that one. But his rise was quite extraordinary. I mean, Drexel's where he worked, their high yield department at one point had four times the capital of Goldman Sachs. According to you and Milken, again, I think you
turns.zh: 是啊，你写到关于 Milken 的那些故事真的很精彩。我是说，你写到他从费城到纽约有长达五小时的通勤，他专门雇了一个人坐在他旁边，好让别人不来打扰他，这样他就能把时间都花在研究债券市场上。这个细节我特别喜欢。但他的崛起相当非凡。他供职的 Drexel，其高收益部门一度拥有高盛（Goldman Sachs）四倍的资本。据你说，而且 Milken，我想你还——

turns.en: say earned 550 million in. 1986 when that was real money. Yeah, I mean even Elon Musk would struggle to get that kind of, of paycheck now. But what I thought was interesting about the Milken example was he goes on to basically create the modern junk bond market. And he does this based on what you just described is under observation that high yield bonds default or the return on a high yield bonds more than compensates for the default risk. But that original paper was written really looking at companies
turns.zh: ——写到他在 1986 年赚了 5.5 亿美元，在那个年代那可是真金白银。是啊，我是说，即便像 Elon Musk 现在也很难拿到那样的薪水。但我觉得 Milken 这个例子里有意思的是，他后来基本上创造出了现代高收益债券市场。他这么做，正是基于你刚才描述的那个观察：高收益债券的回报足以超额补偿其违约风险。但最初那篇论文其实考察的是那些——

turns.en: that were so called fallen angels. In other words, they were companies that issued bonds when they were in stronger conditions and then they became lowly rated. And what Milken did was create an original issue junk bond market. So people were coming to market with junk bonds as opposed to having bond that, you know, that had started off high yield, high, highly rated and became junk bonds. So could you just tell us a little bit about that? Because it's a great example, I think of people studying
turns.zh: ——所谓的'堕落天使'（fallen angels）公司。换句话说，它们是那些在状况较好时发行了债券、随后评级变低的公司。而 Milken 做的，是创造了一个原始发行的高收益债券市场：人们直接带着高收益债券来到市场发行，而不是那种一开始高评级、后来才沦为高收益债券的债券。你能就此给我们讲讲吗？因为我觉得这是个绝佳的例子，说明人们研究——

turns.en: the market, acting on it and then changing the very thing that they've studied.
turns.zh: ——市场、据此行动，然后又改变了他们研究的那个东西本身。

turns.en: Yeah, no, I mean, I think this is also what's unique about him in that, you know, let's say that original Braddock Hickman paper, let's say if a million people had read it, and that's a million people have not read that paper, but let's say 100 people would have understood and grasped the implications. 99 of them would have just used it to buy junk bonds. Just use it as a great investment strategy, it would have made lots of money and that's great. And probably wouldn't known as great investments. Really all they
turns.zh: 是啊，我认为这也正是他的独特之处。比方说 Braddock Hickman 最初那篇论文，假如有 100 万人读过它——当然并没有 100 万人读过——但假设有 100 个人理解并领悟了它的含义。其中 99 个人只会拿它去买高收益债券，把它当成一个很棒的投资策略，会赚很多钱，那很好，可能也会被视为很棒的投资。他们真正做的——

turns.en: did was systematically buy junky bonds and harvest that return premium that you'd get. The hundredth person was Mike Milken and he decided to build something. Like he decided to transform it and in the process change its nature. Because I mean, one of the almost original sins I see in financial economics or in finance all the time is that people treat it as if it's science. Like If I do 100 physical experiments, you're going to get 100 same results. In finance, the market is adaptive, it's dynamic,
turns.zh: ——就是系统性地买入垃圾债券、去收获那份回报溢价。而那第 100 个人是 Mike Milken，他决定去构建点东西。他决定去改造它，并在这个过程中改变了它的本质。因为我在金融经济学、或者说在整个金融领域里经常看到的一个'原罪'是：人们把它当成科学来对待。就好像我做 100 次物理实验，会得到 100 次相同的结果。而在金融里，市场是适应性的、是动态的，

turns.en: it changes. And as somebody discovers something, it generally gets kind of whittled out. And junk bonds, because Mike Milken had studied a period when it was primarily companies like you say, hubby investment graded mid downgraded and a few corporate raiders, that first generation of corporate raiders had issued paper that was, you know, rather pejoratively into, you know, if it equals a Chinese paper at the time. And you know, he decided to make it, yeah, a new issue market. But of course I think that
turns.zh: 它会变化。一旦有人发现了什么，那份收益通常就会被慢慢磨平。而高收益债券这块，因为 Mike Milken 研究的那个时期，主要还是像你说的、由投资级被下调的公司，以及少数企业掠夺者（corporate raiders）——那第一代企业掠夺者——发行的一些债券，当时被颇为贬义地称作（转写不清，大致是'Chinese paper'之类）。他决定把它做成一个——对——新发行市场。但当然，我认为——

turns.en: the first iterations, the first vintages of this market were generally the better companies and the better raiders because he kind of built this entire machinery. He seeded funds. I mean he created not just, I mean the, I mean the whole industry. Industry.
turns.zh: ——这个市场最早的几个版本、最早的几批'年份'（vintages），普遍是较好的公司和较好的掠夺者，因为他搭建起了这整套机器。他为基金提供种子资金。我是说，他创造的不只是——而是整个行业。

turns.en: He's the father of it all. The whole leverage finance industry, even today's private credit, like that's his grandchild and he built the whole thing. But of course, you know, as they found more and more and some of these raiders, you go like some of those were in print. Like a. Carl Icahn is an impressive guy and lots of his stuff didn't work out. But like he's, he's smart. Not all of those raiders were actually very good. And they were just as wasteful as the corporate CEOs that they replaced. So they were
turns.zh: 他是这一切之父。整个杠杆融资（leverage finance）行业，甚至今天的私募信贷（private credit），都算是他的'孙辈'，而整套东西都是他搭建的。但当然，随着他们发得越来越多，其中一些掠夺者——你会说有些是见于报端的，比如 Carl Icahn 是个了不起的人，他的很多操作也没成功，但他确实聪明。可不是所有那些掠夺者都真的很优秀，他们和被他们取代的那些公司 CEO 一样浪费。所以他们——

turns.en: supposedly making corporate America leaner and meaner, but in practice they were just kind of propagating some of the same issues.
turns.zh: ——本应让美国企业变得更精简、更凶悍，但实际上他们只是在延续某些同样的问题。

turns.en: So you can see some of the later vintages of junk defaulted in very high numbers. The returns were not great because that market had evolved. A lot of companies that normally would have been shut out completely had been able to issue. A lot of companies were rightly shut out of the market, were able to issue, thanks to Drexel Burnham Lambert's machinery, this bank where Mike Milken worked. And I think still to this day there is a risk premium in high yield. It's more volatile. It kind of sits between
turns.zh: 所以你能看到，后期那些'年份'的高收益债券违约率高得惊人，回报也不佳，因为那个市场已经演变了。很多本来会被完全挡在门外的公司得以发行债券；很多本该被合理排除在市场之外的公司，也 nhờ Drexel Burnham Lambert 那套机器得以发行——就是 Mike Milken 工作的那家银行。而且我认为，直到今天高收益债券仍存在风险溢价，它波动更大，大致位于——

turns.en: cred like corporate bonds, IG corporate bonds and the equity space. But there is still a premium there. But it waxes and wanes a lot.
turns.zh: ——投资级（IG）公司债和股票之间。但那里仍有一份溢价，只是它会大幅地此消彼长。

turns.en: And it's never been as big as it was when Hickman looked at it.
turns.zh: 而且它从没有像 Hickman 当年研究时那么大过。

turns.en: Yeah, thanks for that, man. I thought that was just such a great example of, I don't know, you call maybe the Soros reflexivity of market right, the individuals changing the fundamentals. I know we're kind of coming down to the end here and I wanted to loop back on this notion of bonds as technology that we've seen these big advances in the use of bonds and their power be linked to the way in which they're structured. And you talk about other technologies that have become very important. Securitization, turning
turns.zh: 是啊，谢谢你的讲解。我觉得这是个绝佳的例子，可以说就是——你也许会称之为 Soros 的市场反身性（reflexivity）吧——个体改变了基本面。我知道我们快到尾声了，我想回到'债券即技术'这个概念上：我们看到债券的用途及其威力的这些重大进步，都与它们的结构设计方式相关联。你还谈到了其他一些变得非常重要的技术，比如证券化（securitization），把——

turns.en: pools of loans into a tradable bond tranching, allowing those pools to be sliced up and structured as cash flows. We know that played both those things, played a big role in the global financial crisis. I wanted to ask two questions. One is where do you see fixed income ETFs on that kind of technology spectrum, number one.
turns.zh: ——贷款池变成可交易的债券；分层（tranching），让这些池子被切分并结构化为现金流。我们知道这两样东西都在全球金融危机中扮演了重要角色。我想问两个问题。第一，你怎么看待固定收益 ETF 处在那条'技术光谱'上的位置？

turns.en: And number two, are there technologies, you know, coming down the pipe that maybe our people are experimenting with or that, you know, we should be kind of keeping our eye on that would have the potential to change the bond market further in the, in the future?
turns.zh: 第二，有没有一些正在酝酿中的技术，也许人们正在试验，或者我们应该持续关注、未来有可能进一步改变债券市场的？

turns.en: Well, if I do the second question first, I still think it's probably a little bit overhyped in certain circles, but some of my smarter contacts are getting quite excited about tokenization or fixed income markets. So we've already seen it in repo. I mean, repo is a fast paced market that kind of underpins everything.
turns.zh: 嗯，我先回答第二个问题。我仍然认为它在某些圈子里可能有点被过度炒作，但我一些更聪明的联系人对固定收益市场的代币化（tokenization）变得相当兴奋。我们已经在回购（repo）市场看到了它。回购是个节奏很快、几乎支撑着一切的市场。

turns.en: I always call it the dark matter of finance because it kind of binds everything together even though you can't see it there. The volumes in tokenized repo, there have been some experts, they're actually growing.
turns.zh: 我一直称它为金融的'暗物质'（dark matter of finance），因为它把一切都绑定在一起，尽管你看不到它。代币化回购的交易量——有些数据显示——其实正在增长。

turns.en: And so just for listeners who aren't aware, how would you describe tokenization of bond markets? Say, well, essentially sort of slicing individual bonds into and trading over distributed ledger. So it's of simultaneous real time trading on a transparent blockchain of some kind. And then you can, you know, the issue with bonds, you can trade it in all sorts of different prices and you know, some of them can be quite tricky to trade. But if you tokenize everything and essentially
turns.zh: 那么，为了那些不了解的听众，你会怎么描述债券市场的代币化？嗯，本质上就是把单只债券切分，并通过分布式账本（distributed ledger）进行交易，也就是在某种透明的区块链（blockchain）上进行同步的实时交易。然后你就可以——你知道，债券的问题在于，它可能以各种不同价格成交，有些还挺难交易的。但如果你把一切都代币化、本质上——

turns.en: turn into like small tradable units, it should make liquidity better. It should make trading easier, more efficient. You don't have to of T +3 settlement days like if I buy a bond, if I buy muni bond, I think quite often you still have to wait 30 days until you actually kind of hit the account. It's just some parts of the bond market are still very much stuck in the 20th century. But I'm not an expert on tokenization. But it's One of those areas I've started
turns.zh: ——把它变成小的可交易单元，那应该会改善流动性，让交易更容易、更高效。你就不必忍受 T+3 的结算日——比如如果我买一只债券、买一只市政债券（muni bond），我想很多时候你甚至还得等 30 天才真正到账。只是债券市场的某些部分仍然严重停留在 20 世纪。但我不是代币化方面的专家。不过它是我开始——

turns.en: to think I should pay a bit more attention to and think about the implications because if it does look make fixed income a bit more equity like as well and the speed and efficiency that has implications for how like literally the, the nature of the market changes it evolves. And that actually leads to the second issue which is a subject close to my heart. I've written an entire book on the history of, of index funds and ETFs and I, I would say I for a very long time not underestimate I I always thought
turns.zh: ——觉得应该多关注、多思考其影响的领域之一，因为如果它确实能让固定收益变得更像股票一点，那种速度和效率就会实实在在地影响市场本质如何变化、如何演化。而这其实引出了第二个话题，是个我特别上心的题目。我写过一整本关于指数基金（index funds）和 ETF 历史的书，我可以说，很长一段时间里我都没低估——我一直认为

turns.en: passive would have another sort of similar arc in fixed income as it has had in equities that I've been so sure about for a long time. I've written lots about for the FT and in my book but what I had underappreciated is how specifically the technology of the ETF for want of a better word but the creation, redemption process kind of how that kind of structure operates is both probably arguably better for less liquid markets like the fixed income markets which I, you know there's always been this worry about
turns.zh: ——被动投资（passive）在固定收益里会走出跟在股票里类似的另一条弧线，这一点我长期以来非常确信，也为《金融时报》（FT）和我的书写过很多。但我此前低估的，是 ETF 这项技术——暂且这么说——具体而言是它的创设、赎回（creation, redemption）流程、那种结构如何运作，其实可以说对流动性较差的市场、比如固定收益市场更有利；而你知道，一直以来人们都担心——

turns.en: the, the combination of less traded underlying securities and a highly tradable equity wrapper that they would collide in ways that are bad. And I've actually gone from sharing a general oh this I'm sure this will end badly at some point or there will be something bad that happens to actually think the ETF might be in a better wrapper at least for many investors in fixed income markets. And also I'd radically underestimate how much that technology is kind of almost unlocked or sped up or interacted
turns.zh: ——交易不活跃的底层证券与一个高度可交易的股票式外壳（wrapper）组合在一起，会以糟糕的方式相互冲突。而实际上，我已经从原来那种'我敢肯定这迟早会以糟糕收场、或会出什么乱子'的普遍看法，转变为真的认为：ETF 也许是一个更好的外壳，至少对固定收益市场里的很多投资者来说是这样。而且我还严重低估了这项技术在多大程度上几乎解锁了、加速了、或以有趣的方式 interacted——

turns.en: in interesting ways with other fixed income trends like the electronification of bond markets. So more is being traded electronically. The old days we did everything by the phone. It's kind of of they're definitely dying in things like treasury which have been very electronic for a while but also credit is becoming more electronic.
turns.zh: ——与其他固定收益趋势相互作用，比如债券市场的电子化（electronification）。越来越多的交易以电子方式进行。过去我们什么都靠电话，而现在那种方式在国债（treasury）这类早已高度电子化的品种里肯定正在消亡，信用债（credit）也在变得越来越电子化。

turns.en: Then you have the rise of portfolio trading where you can trade big blocks of bonds like massive lines of QIPs, you know, tens, hundreds, even thousands of bonds. Sometimes the ETF is perfect for that because you can sort of if it looks a little bit like one of the ETFs you can very easy to strip out a portfolio from that or create a portfolio from an ETF share. And then there's systematic trading. I know lots of stat arb hedge fund types in the hedge fund space at quants. It's kind of one of my first
turns.zh: 然后是组合交易（portfolio trading）的兴起，你可以一次交易大块债券，比如巨量的 CUSIPs，几十、几百甚至几千只债券。有时候 ETF 非常适合这个，因为如果它看上去有点像某只 ETF，你就能很容易地从中拆出一个组合，或者用 ETF 份额构建一个组合。还有系统化交易（systematic trading）。我认识很多对冲基金里的统计套利（stat arb）型量化人士。这算是我最早的——

turns.en: loves as a financial journalist. I think it's fascinating and there's been talk for at least 10, 15 years that fixed income will have the same quant revolution that happened in equity markets. And it hasn't really materialized to the same extent.
turns.zh: ——作为财经记者的爱好之一。我觉得它很迷人，而且至少十到十五年来一直有人说，固定收益会迎来跟股票市场相同的量化革命。但它并没有真的在同等程度上实现。

turns.en: But I think the ETF, because of it kind of the ETFs makes a lot of bonds more liquid. More liquid bonds leads to more trading, more trading leads to narrow bid ask spreads. It kind of starts like, it's like, I know I'm going to sound like a McKinsey consultant here, but it's like a flywheel where it's all, it's all helping each other. And the crucial change was the etf. And the etf, contrary to what people, including me, fear that it would cause an accident and would, would be bad for the liquidity of
turns.zh: 但我认为 ETF——因为它让很多债券更具流动性。更具流动性的债券带来更多交易，更多交易带来更窄的买卖价差（bid-ask spread）。这有点像——我知道我这么说会像个麦肯锡（McKinsey）顾问——它像一个飞轮（flywheel），各环节互相促进。而那个关键变化就是 ETF。ETF 恰恰相反于人们（包括我）曾担心的、以为它会引发事故、会损害债券——

turns.en: the bond market. Remember, for a long time we worried about the liquidity of the bond market. The tradability of it was dying in the wake of the reforms of the financial crisis. In fact, the etf, I'd argue, has helped save the bond market. It has helped make large parts of the credit markets especially far more liquid than they've ever been before. And it has other unintended consequences. Like if you're not in an index, if you are issuing a bond that doesn't
turns.zh: ——市场流动性的担忧。要知道，长期以来我们都担心债券市场的流动性，在金融危机后的改革余波中，它的可交易性正在消亡。而事实上，我要说，ETF 帮助拯救了债券市场，它帮助让信用债市场（credit markets）的很大一部分变得比以往任何时候都更具流动性。它还有其他的意外后果：比如如果你不在某个指数里，如果你发行的一只债券看起来——

turns.en: plausibly fit into one of the major indices that is used by one of the major ETFs, then you're kind of a bit of an ugly stepchild.
turns.zh: ——不太可能合理地纳入某只主要 ETF 所用的那些主要指数之一，那你就有点像是个'丑小鸭继子'（ugly stepchild）。

turns.en: The liquidity is pools, right? It centers around something. But I think the etf, and there is not a chapter in my book about this, I mentioned this, but I've written a lot about it for the Financial Times, but I think is genuinely one of the more interesting trends to watch over the next five years is the, the ecosystem shift in fixed income, especially credit, which has been slightly more archaic and how ETFs are actually speeding that up.
turns.zh: 流动性是成池的，对吧？它会围绕某些东西聚集。但我认为 ETF——我书里没有专门一章讲这个，我提到过，但我为《金融时报》写过很多——它确实是未来五年里最值得关注的趋势之一：固定收益（尤其是相对更陈旧的信用债）里的生态系统转变，以及 ETF 实际上正在加速这一转变。

turns.en: And I'm sure we will have accents at some point, but that's been fascinating to watch.
turns.zh: 我确信中间肯定会有些事故（accidents，转写作 accents），但看着这一切演变一直很迷人。

turns.en: Yeah, I completely agree. And it's had the effect of making a lot of different bonds more money. Like, you know, and, you know, the.
turns.zh: 是啊，我完全同意。它的效果是让很多不同的债券更具货币性（more money-like）。就像，你知道，那个——

turns.en: No, we won't, we won't go. That's a different rabbit hole. But yeah, I love rabbit holes though, Kevin. Rabbit holes are the best. My life is a whole rabbit hole, basically.
turns.zh: 不，我们不往那走，那是另一个'兔子洞'（rabbit hole）了。不过是啊，我很喜欢兔子洞，Kevin。兔子洞最棒了。我这辈子基本上就是个大大的兔子洞。

turns.en: Like I wrote a book about my last rabbit hole. Well, let's, let's maybe wrap up. I can't let you off the hook without asking you about what's currently going on in the bond market. And as we're recording this at the end of August2020,
turns.zh: 我就为我上一个兔子洞写了一本书。好，那我们也许来收个尾吧。在放你走之前，我得问问你眼下债券市场正在发生什么。我们录制这期节目是在 2020 年 8 月底——

turns.en: and this is just after Scott Besant, the Treasury Secretary, has kind of doubled the size of the treasury liquidity enhancing buybacks. And there's been a lot of criticism of that and a different explanation for what he's trying to do. You've just written an excellent piece on the, I don't know, the dependence of the US bond market on hedge funds now. And that relates to hedge funds increasing their footprint, their owning of treasury bonds as part of a variety of arbitrage strategies, the most important of
turns.zh: ——就在那之前不久，财政部长 Scott Bessent（转写作 Besant）刚刚把国债流动性增强型回购（buybacks）的规模大致翻了一倍。对此有很多批评，也有对他意图的不同解读。你刚写了一篇很棒的文章，讲的是——我不知道怎么说——如今美国债券市场对对冲基金（hedge funds）的依赖。这与对冲基金扩大其足迹、增持国债有关，这是各种套利策略的一部分，其中最重要的——

turns.en: which is the so called basis trade where they go long the physical bonds and they short the futures trying to, and they lever up the difference in price between those two things. So as part of that they are big buyers of treasury bonds. And the book that I write and talk about, that I wrote and I talk about is the rise of carry. And that trade is essentially a carry trade. It has all the characteristics of carry, it's highly levered, it's liquidity providing and it tends to do poorly in periods of
turns.zh: ——就是所谓的基差交易（basis trade）：他们做多实物债券、做空期货，试图对两者之间的价差加杠杆。所以作为其中一环，他们是国债的大买家。而我写过、也常常谈及的那本书讲的是'套息（carry）的崛起'。那笔交易本质上就是一笔套息交易，它具备套息的所有特征：高杠杆、提供流动性，而且往往在——

turns.en: high volatility. So it's short volatility. So my thesis, or not really my thesis, but a thesis that people have put out there, is that what Bessant is trying to do with these buybacks is to kind of cap the volatility on the bond market and therefore kind of make it safer for these basis traders to continue buying treasury bonds. And I think the evidence for that is we don't really have enough data, I think to say conclusively. But what do you think, what do you think is the idea, the motivation behind what
turns.zh: ——高波动时期表现不佳，所以它是做空波动率（short volatility）。所以我的论点——或者说并非真是我的论点，而是人们提出的一种论点——是：Bessent 想通过这些回购做的，就是给债券市场的波动率封顶，从而让这些基差交易者能更安全地继续买入国债。而我认为，要断定这一点的证据——我们其实还没有足够的数据来下结论。但你怎么看？你觉得他这么做背后的想法、动机是什么——

turns.en: Besant has been doing with the buybacks? Well, I've thought a lot about this and obviously I don't know when this is going out, but I feel very confident in saying that whatever this pod goes out, he will not succeed. The buybacks, increasing those buybacks, Even if he 10x's it, it's like peeing on a forest fire. It is not going to have a meaningful impact. And the bond market has sussed that out very quickly after the initial shock.
turns.zh: ——就用这些回购在做的这件事？嗯，我对此想了很多。显然我不知道这期节目什么时候播出，但我可以非常有把握地说：无论这期节目何时上线，他都不会成功。增加这些回购——哪怕他把它扩大 10 倍，那也像是对着森林大火撒尿，不会有实质影响。而债券市场在最初的震惊之后，很快就看清了这一点。

turns.en: There are other levers he can do, but fundamentally every dollar the US treasury spends is a dollar they have to borrow. They're just switching $1 for another dollar of debt. And you can change the maturity structure and issue lots of treasury bills to pay for long dated buybacks, but again, give them the scale of what the US Government is borrowing. It's not going to materially change. Nothing's going to help. I do agree that he wanted to bring Back that low end and make of dampen down volatility. But
turns.zh: 他还有别的杠杆可用，但从根本上说，美国财政部每花一美元，就得借一美元。他们只是把 1 美元的债务换成另 1 美元的债务。你可以改变期限结构、发行大量国库券（treasury bills）来为长期限回购融资，但同样，考虑到美国政府借款的规模，这不会带来实质改变，什么都帮不上。我确实同意他想把长端拉回来、想压一压波动率。但——

turns.en: what I just don't get is that the volatility was not high. There was a bit of a sell off. This is not after Liberation Day in 2025 when the bond market, it was more of a swap spread reds trade blow up than a basis trade blow up. But I think they were quite rightly worried that the basis trade would be the next big shoot to drop. There are already signs of weakness in some of the weaker players in that trade because there's so much money tied up in that. So then they kind of, Trump famously said the bond
turns.zh: ——我就是想不通的是，波动率当时并不高。只是有一点抛售。这跟 2025 年'解放日'之后的情况不一样，当时债券市场更像是一场掉期利差交易（swap spread）的爆仓，而不是基差交易的爆仓。但我认为他们担心基差交易会是下一只落下的靴子，这担心相当合理。因为那笔交易里锁住了太多钱，其中一些较弱的参与者已经显现出疲态。于是他们——Trump 曾著名地说债券——

turns.en: market was getting yippee and they put a pause, took a timeout on the, on the tariffs until things calmed down again. But this was not a fantastically volatile era. It was just like inflation. People were pricing and inflation was probably going to stay a little bit more elevated for a bit longer. And the Federal Reserve looks under new management and the chairmanship of Kevin Ward less inclined to raise interest rates. So this is a credibility issue.
turns.zh: ——市场变得'yippee'（转写不清，指市场情绪化、失控），于是他们按下了暂停键，对关税叫了个暂停，直到局势重新平静下来。但这并不是一个波动极其剧烈的时期。只是通胀——人们在定价通胀，而通胀大概会在更高位停留更久一点。而且美联储（Federal Reserve）在新管理层、在 Kevin Warsh（转写作 Kevin Ward）的主席任下，看上去更不愿意加息。所以这是个信誉（credibility）问题。

turns.en: So you can see the term premium was going up, inflation breaking, it wasn't changing that much. But the simplest solution is just for Kevin Walsh to say that he's up for interest rate increases and you'll see that calm down. So it feels like, you know, it's like that old ad age, I can't remember what, where it's from, but it's like we must do something. This is something. Ergo we do this and it doesn't really work. So they felt they had to do something. Affordability is an issue. 30 year mortgages were
turns.zh: 所以你能看到期限溢价（term premium）在上升，通胀预期（breakeven）并没怎么变化。但最简单的解决办法，就是让 Kevin Warsh 表态说他愿意加息，你就会看到局面平静下来。所以这感觉就像那句老话——我记不清出自哪里了——'我们必须做点什么。这就是个办法。所以我们做这个'，可它其实并不管用。于是他们觉得必须做点什么。负担能力（affordability）是个问题，30 年期房贷当时正——

turns.en: getting more expensive. We must do something. This is something.
turns.zh: ——变得越来越贵。我们必须做点什么。这就是个办法。

turns.en: Well, actually just makes you seem incoherent and desperate, but it's something at least. So I struggle to see the rationale beyond.
turns.zh: 嗯，其实这么做只会让你显得语无伦次、走投无路，但至少算是做了点什么。所以我很难看出 beyond 这之外还有什么道理。

turns.en: Bessant knows all this, I'm sure, I'm sure he knows this was not going to work. I think he just did it because the boss man wanted him to do something. And this was something. And it's going to be interesting to see how they evolve and how they do this.
turns.zh: Bessent 这一切都清楚，我确信他知道这不会奏效。我觉得他这么做只是因为'老板'想让他做点什么，而这就算是做了点什么。接下来他们如何演变、如何做这件事，会很有意思。

turns.en: But fundamentally, if inflation is going to stay higher for longer and we still, I mean it's been quite a while since and this isn't just under Walsh or Trump, of course, but inflation has been above the Federal Reserve's target for quite a while now and they've talked about the difficulty of that last mile.
turns.zh: 但从根本上说，如果通胀要在更高位停留更久——而且我们已经——我是说，这不只是在 Warsh 或 Trump 任下的事，通胀已经高于美联储目标相当长一段时间了，他们也谈到过'最后一公里'（last mile）的艰难。

turns.en: Well, I think the Federal Reserve now needs to walk it. And if that walk falls on Kevin Walsh, and that is awkward for him in his position and he's probably promised Trump that he doesn't want to raise interest rates. I think they should just sell it as if Trump wants lower 30 year mortgage rates. This is the easiest way of doing it. That really, if you're raising interest rate, it doesn't really matter that much, but you are essentially making mortgages more affordable and maybe that's what
turns.zh: 嗯，我认为美联储现在需要走完这最后一公里。如果这一步落在了 Kevin Warsh 身上，那对他这个位置来说会很尴尬，而且他大概已经向 Trump 承诺过不想加息。我觉得他们就该这么去推销：如果 Trump 想要更低的 30 年期房贷利率，这就是最简单的办法。其实，如果你在加息，那也没那么要紧，但你本质上是在让房贷更可负担，也许这就是——

turns.en: they do. We'll see in the coming weeks and months. Yeah, it'll be fascinating. I'm not optimistic that they'll be able to walk that last mile, but as you say, we'll see. Well, listen, Robin, that's a good place to wrap up. We really appreciate you taking the time. It's a fascinating book and we wish you all the best with the launch.
turns.zh: ——他们会做的。未来几周、几个月就见分晓了。是啊，那会很精彩。我并不乐观他们能走完那最后一公里，但就像你说的，我们拭目以待。好，听着，Robin，这是个收尾的好节点。非常感谢你抽出时间。这是一本迷人的书，祝新书发布一切顺利。

turns.en: No thanks, Kevin. I really appreciate that. And yeah, I love being here and I've been looking forward to it.
turns.zh: 哪里，谢谢你，Kevin。我非常感激。是啊，我很喜欢来这里，我一直很期待。

It's out September 29th 9th and make sure to get a copy. As always, what we've talked today really is just a tiny fraction of what you're going to learn from the book. It's really worthwhile, it's fun, and I recommend it. So that's it for today for all of us here at Top Traders Unplugged. Thanks for listening and we'll see you next time.
